title: Don't let our hearts swerve
hookLine: our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You guided us (3:8)
last: SOME VERSES ARE FOR SITTING WITH.

cards: Yesterday's verse carried a warning: some have a swerve in their hearts, and chase what's unclear. The very next verse doesn't point a finger at them. It turns around and asks for help.
Commentators hear the people just praised, those firmly rooted in knowledge, as the ones speaking. Their first worry isn't other people's hearts. It's their own.
If anyone could feel safe from drifting, it's them. They don't.

teach.b: In Pickthall's translation, 3:8 begins: "Our Lord! Cause not our hearts to stray after Thou hast guided us." Then it asks for mercy from God's own presence, and ends: You are the Bestower. Notice the link.
Yesterday's verse said zaygh, a swerve, in the hearts of some. Today's asks la tuzigh, don't let them swerve.
Same root, z-y-gh: to lean, to tilt away from straight. One verse describes the tilt; the next asks to be kept from it.
Notice the timing too: after You guided us. It's a prayer for people who've already found the way and know that finding it once isn't the same as staying on it.
A hadith in Tirmidhi reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ often said: O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon your religion.
Anas, who reports it, says the companions asked whether he feared for them, and he said yes: hearts are held between two of God's fingers, and He turns them as He wills.
Turner of hearts is muqallib al-qulub, and both words share one root, q-l-b, to turn over: the heart is named as the thing that turns.

teach.h: OUR LORD! CAUSE NOT OUR HEARTS TO STRAY.
teach.b: Some Muslims say 3:8 in their supplications after the prayer.
And it closes a week about keeping things: a man raised after a hundred years, a grain that multiplies, a gift unspoiled, a debt written down, a burden that fits, verses held firm or held open.

how: Many Muslims say the supplication of 3:8, 'rabbana la tuzigh qulubana', after the daily prayers and in personal du'a, along with the Prophet's reported prayer to the Turner of hearts.

o: a swerve, a heart tilting away from straight
a hidden meaning in an unclear verse
a heart that has turned hard as stone

games.q: don't let our hearts swerve — tap the pairs.

s: 3:8 is a prayer for people who are lost
it asks God not to let hearts swerve after You guided us: it's for people already on the way.
one describes a swerve in the heart; the next asks to be kept from it.
the Prophet never worried about his own heart
Tirmidhi reports he often asked the Turner of hearts to keep his heart firm.

games.q: you've just heard a verse warning about people whose hearts swerve. the next verse is spoken by the faithful. what do they say?
o: at least we're not like them.
our Lord, don't let our hearts swerve after You guided us.
explain the hard verses to us now.
games.why: they ask for their own hearts to be kept straight. the verse turns from describing others to a request about ourselves.

practice: Sit up straight and feel how small the movements are that keep you upright, a lean forward, a correction back; nobody sits perfectly still.
Think of one place this week where your heart tilted a little, toward impatience, envy or carelessness, and without scolding it, notice the lean and come back to center.
If you pray, you can say 3:8 in Arabic or your own language: rabbana la tuzigh qulubana.

wordCard.voice: Zaygh, a swerve in the heart. The request of 3:8, la tuzigh, asks not to let it happen, made by people already guided, who want to stay that way. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: our Lord, do not let our hearts swerve (3:8).

carryVoice: Your line: keep my heart straight. A lean you notice is a lean you can correct. That's a week, done.
